Name: OpenAPI Code Generation
Strategy: Generate server interfaces and client SDKs from a versioned OpenAPI description
Tooling: OpenAPI Generator; custom templates; selective generation
Strengths: Shared interface description; repeatable client generation; documentation derived from the same input
Weaknesses: Generator and language support varies; generated output still needs tests; runtime implementation can drift
When to Use: Teams with multiple client platforms consuming the same API; public APIs with external consumers
Gotcha: Pin generator and templates; verify regenerated output in CI; committing generated code is a repository policy rather than a universal prohibition

Name: GraphQL Federation
Strategy: Compose subgraph schemas into a supergraph with metadata for routing client operations
Tooling: Apollo Federation; GraphOS; Rover supergraph compose
Strengths: Independent subgraph ownership; unified client schema; composition catches conflicting definitions
Weaknesses: Composition and routing add operational complexity; cross-subgraph execution needs performance testing
When to Use: Services with separately owned domains that need one GraphQL contract
Gotcha: Successful composition checks subgraph consistency rather than proving compatibility with existing client operations or runtime resolver behavior

Name: Schema Evolution (Backward Compatible)
Strategy: Preserve old-client requests and response expectations; assess generated source and binary wire and JSON compatibility separately
Tooling: Buf breaking with FILE or PACKAGE or WIRE_JSON or WIRE; consumer verification
Strengths: Compatible changes can reduce coordinated upgrades within an explicitly supported version policy
Weaknesses: Additive changes can still break consumers; schema checks do not prove unchanged behavior; deprecation needs migration planning
When to Use: APIs with many consumers who cannot coordinate upgrades; long-lived public APIs
Gotcha: New required inputs reject old requests; new response enum values can break exhaustive clients; new JSON fields can fail closed readers; deprecation alone does not make removal safe

Name: API Versioning via URL Path
Strategy: Expose incompatible contracts at distinct paths such as /v1/users and /v2/users while maintaining supported old routes
Strengths: Visible version selection; straightforward routing; distinct URI cache keys
Weaknesses: Multiple contracts and routes to maintain; version sprawl; links must target the correct version
When to Use: Public or internal APIs whose consumers need independent migration windows
Gotcha: Internal APIs can need versioning too; a new path does not preserve old behavior automatically; maintain old response shapes and semantics until retirement

Name: API Versioning via Headers
Strategy: Select versions using a documented custom header or vendor media type such as Accept: application/vnd.contoso.v2+json
Strengths: Stable resource URLs; explicit representation negotiation; multiple contracts on one path
Weaknesses: Less visible version selection; negotiation and cache configuration add complexity
When to Use: APIs that need stable resource URLs and clients able to send explicit version preferences
Gotcha: For cacheable variants emit Vary for the selecting header and verify CDN cache keys; Accept is not inherently uncacheable; JSON:API 1.1 permits only ext and profile media type parameters

Name: Contract Testing
Strategy: Generate contracts from consumer tests and verify them against providers; distinguish this from provider-only schema conformance
Tooling: Pact; Pact Broker verification matrix; can-i-deploy
Strengths: Detects mismatches in exercised interactions; supports independent deployments using version-specific evidence
Weaknesses: Only represented consumer interactions are covered; provider states and verification results require maintenance
When to Use: Inter-service HTTP or message integrations with independently released consumers and providers
Gotcha: Publish consumer contracts and provider results with exact versions; gate against the target environment and record deployments or releases; passing tests do not certify unrepresented consumers or all API behavior

Name: Protobuf Schema Registry
Strategy: Publish versioned protobuf modules and dependencies with explicitly configured compatibility checks
Tooling: Buf Schema Registry; Buf CLI; registry-side checks
Strengths: Schema discovery; versioned dependencies; generated SDK distribution; enforcement of selected breaking-change rules
Weaknesses: Registry and policy administration; rule coverage depends on compatibility category; schema checks do not prove application behavior
When to Use: gRPC services and shared protobuf libraries needing governed schema distribution
Gotcha: Never reuse field numbers; reserve removed numbers and names; binary-safe changes can break generated code or ProtoJSON; old JSON readers reject new fields by default so sequence reader and writer rollout

Name: AsyncAPI for Event-Driven APIs
Strategy: Describe message contracts and channels separately from application send and receive operations in AsyncAPI 3
Tooling: AsyncAPI converter; AsyncAPI-compatible documentation and generation tools
Strengths: Reusable channel and message definitions; explicit operation direction; protocol-specific bindings
Weaknesses: Specification migration requires tooling checks; documentation alone does not enforce message compatibility or delivery guarantees
When to Use: Event-driven APIs that need shared message documentation and generation inputs
Gotcha: In v3 channel keys are identifiers rather than addresses and operations use action: send or receive from the application's perspective; a v2-to-v3 document conversion is not proof of payload compatibility

Name: BFF (Backend for Frontend) Pattern
Strategy: Create frontend-owned APIs that tailor aggregation and client-specific logic to each user experience
Tooling: Custom BFF services; frontend-specific GraphQL resolvers; Azure Functions
Strengths: Client-tailored payloads; independent frontend release cadence; reduced exposure to backend topology
Weaknesses: Extra service lifecycle and security work; possible code duplication; added network latency
When to Use: Multiple interfaces with meaningfully different needs and frontend teams able to own their backend layer
Gotcha: Client-specific logic is appropriate in a BFF; keep shared domain rules in owning services and avoid separate BFFs when interfaces have the same needs

Name: API Gateway Pattern
Strategy: Use a managed entry point to route requests and apply cross-cutting policies; optionally aggregate calls
Tooling: Azure API Management; reverse proxies; service mesh ingress gateways
Strengths: Simpler client endpoints; centralized authentication and rate limits; backend topology abstraction
Weaknesses: Extra hop and policy complexity; shared routing failures can affect many consumers; capacity and availability need design
When to Use: APIs needing shared routing or edge policies across multiple backend services
Gotcha: Gateways can aggregate and transform rather than only route; review policy and routing changes as contract changes and keep shared business workflows in owning services

Name: gRPC-Web
Strategy: Expose protobuf RPCs to browser clients through a gRPC-Web-capable proxy or server
Tooling: grpc-web; Envoy; server frameworks with gRPC-Web support
Strengths: Shared protobuf messages and service stubs; unary calls; server streaming with the supported transport mode
Weaknesses: Official grpc-web client lacks client and bidirectional streaming; transport and proxy behavior need integration tests
When to Use: Full-stack teams using protobuf who want type consistency from browser to backend
Gotcha: Official grpc-web supports server streaming only in grpcwebtext mode and binary grpcweb mode is unary-only; WebSocket fallback is not a standard gRPC-Web capability

Name: Hypermedia APIs (HATEOAS)
Strategy: Expose links and documented relation semantics so clients can discover related resources and supported transitions
Tooling: JSON:API links and relationships; hypermedia-aware clients
Strengths: Less hardcoded URI construction; discoverable relationships; links can coexist with OpenAPI descriptions
Weaknesses: Clients still need media type and relation semantics; link traversal and representation design add complexity
When to Use: Resource-oriented APIs whose clients benefit from runtime navigation
Gotcha: Links alone do not guarantee backward compatibility; preserve relation meanings and payload contracts; JSON:API relationship self links and related resource links have different semantics

Name: JSON Schema Contract Evolution
Strategy: Declare object requirements and unknown-property policy; compare accepted requests and emitted responses separately
Tooling: Dialect-aware JSON Schema validators; old and new payload fixtures
Strengths: Makes presence and closed-object constraints explicit; enables reproducible compatibility counterexamples
Weaknesses: Validation describes accepted instances rather than all business semantics; closed schemas restrict extension
When to Use: JSON APIs or event payloads with independently upgraded producers and consumers
Gotcha: Properties are optional unless required; null is not absence; new fields fail old additionalProperties: false readers; additionalProperties sees only its own subschema while unevaluatedProperties can account for successful subschema evaluation

Name: OpenAPI 3.1 Schema Dialects
Strategy: Treat OpenAPI 3.1 Schema Objects as a JSON Schema 2020-12-based dialect and declare overrides explicitly
Tooling: OpenAPI 3.1-aware validators and generators; JSON Schema 2020-12 tooling
Strengths: Reusable schema vocabulary; explicit dialect selection; support for null as a type
Weaknesses: Generator and validator support varies; annotations need application-specific handling
When to Use: Teams sharing schemas across HTTP descriptions and JSON Schema validation pipelines
Gotcha: Schema-root $schema overrides jsonSchemaDialect; format is non-validating by default; readOnly and writeOnly are annotations; discriminator does not change oneOf validation; changing openapi or info.version does not route API traffic

Name: Protobuf Field Presence
Strategy: Use explicit presence when an omitted scalar must differ from an explicitly supplied default value
Tooling: Proto3 optional; editions explicit presence; FieldMask for partial updates
Strengths: Distinguishes unset from zero or false; explicitly set defaults participate in merge operations
Weaknesses: Repeated fields and maps do not track presence; mixed implicit and explicit peers can lose presence on round trips
When to Use: Partial-update RPCs and contracts where absence differs from a default scalar value
Gotcha: Implicit-presence defaults are omitted and skipped by merge; wire-compatible presence changes can still break semantics when an older peer reserializes an explicitly set default

Name: gRPC Deadline and Cancellation Contracts
Strategy: Set realistic client deadlines and propagate remaining budgets to downstream RPCs; stop application work on cancellation
Tooling: gRPC deadline APIs; cancellation contexts; status codes
Strengths: Bounds client waiting; propagates caller time budgets; enables cancellation-aware resource cleanup
Weaknesses: No deadline by default; propagation defaults vary by language; application tasks must cooperate with cancellation
When to Use: RPC chains requiring bounded waits and explicit timeout behavior
Gotcha: DEADLINE_EXCEEDED can occur after a state-changing operation succeeds; cancellation does not imply rollback; retries of non-idempotent operations need a deduplication or reconciliation strategy
